A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MOLM with the same authors, core method, and experimental framework. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–E support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original watermark detection, image-quality, attack-robustness, and ablation results on Stable Diffusion and FLUX, including substantial appendix experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds reported user-attribution results, baseline comparisons, SD 3.5 results, and heterogeneous-message averaging-attack results.

M1.justification: The key-dependent LoRA routing, frozen backbone, extractor, and perceptual-plus-binary-cross-entropy objective remain unchanged. Appendix B.1 revises the perceptual-loss reference to the generated non-watermarked image, bringing its description into agreement with Equation 2 already present in v1; this does not establish an algorithm change.

E1.justification: v2 adds an evaluated multi-user attribution task with rejection of non-watermarked inputs, using 1,000 registered users; v1 described attribution conceptually but reported detection and bit recovery. MS-COCO and LAION-Aesthetics coverage is retained. The SD 3.5 addition expands model configurations within the existing image-generation task.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds TrustMark Q and VINE-R as post-hoc comparators. It also adds Stable Signature, WOUAF, Tree-Ring, and Gaussian-Shading to the LAION comparison, which previously contained only MOLM, and Stable Signature to the FLUX comparison. Existing SD/MS-COCO comparators remain.

E3.justification: The new attribution protocol uses 10,000 watermarked images, 20,000 non-watermarked images, a 27-of-28-bit acceptance threshold, and separate false-positive, true-accept, and conditional-attribution metrics. v2 also evaluates SD 3.5. Appendix B.1 changes the stated training budget from 10K to 12K steps; the PDFs do not establish whether retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Table 2 examines attribution acceptance and correctness under distortions. Appendix C.1 adds explicit heterogeneous-message averaging-removal curves for an attack setting already discussed in v1. The existing augmentation, PGD, U-Net, capacity, mapping, sampler, and rank analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version adds run-to-run uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, error bars, or comparative significance tests. The 100-prompt averaging for mapping heatmaps and qualitative references to different attacker-training seeds remain unchanged. New attribution sample sizes and outcome rates are evaluation-protocol additions.

E6.justification: New attribution results include 98.92% undistorted true acceptance, 100% conditional attribution accuracy, and 0.02% empirical false positives. Table 1 adds comparator results and SD 3.5 results, including FID 26.2 and clean bit accuracy 0.91. New Figure 5 reports heterogeneous-message removal accuracy around 0.88–0.95. Matched earlier numerical results are retained, so these additions do not demonstrate same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Section 4.3 changes the false-positive tail from P(D > τ) to P(s ≥ τ), aligning it with the stated inclusive detection rule, and removes the earlier incomplete-beta expression. The method equations and substantive appendix mathematics remain unchanged; no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: Both versions claim a general parameter-perturbation watermarking framework and its MOLM instantiation, with key changes without retraining, scalable capacity, preserved fidelity, and robustness. The rewritten conclusion reiterates claims already made in v1. The attribution experiments support an existing claimed application.

C2.justification: v2 adds an interpretation of attribution errors as predominantly rejection and discusses the false-positive versus false-negative threshold tradeoff. It corrects the main-text rank interpretation to improved fidelity at higher ranks, although the table caption retains the contrary statement. Inference overhead is qualified as negligible instead of absent.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link in the abstract and revises Appendix B.1's training-step count and perceptual-loss reference. It removes v1's reproducibility statement, including the assertion that comparisons used public codebases. The optimizer, learning rate, batch size, weight decay, loss weight, and A100 training-time disclosure remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for TrustMark, VINE, the compression attackers, and the training-data source. It replaces the HiDDeN citation to Saha et al. with Zhu et al. and removes categorical statements about competing methods lacking key recovery or requiring deterministic sampling. The central positioning relative to LoRA and mixture-of-experts research remains unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized wording and terminology edits, adds the attribution subsection, rewrites the conclusion, condenses Appendix C.2, and removes the reproducibility statement. Headers change from a preprint designation to ICLR 2026 publication. The overall narrative and appendix organization remain recognizable.

P2.justification: The central comparison table is substantially expanded and regrouped, including a post-hoc-method section. v2 adds an attribution table, a heterogeneous-message attack plot, and SD 3.5 image comparisons. It also transposes the retained capacity examples from configuration rows into columns and revises table styling and captions. Existing schematics and image examples are otherwise retained.

improvement.justification: The attribution evaluation and expanded LAION/FLUX comparisons better substantiate applications that v1 supported less directly, while the code pointer and corrected explanations improve usability. Reporting inconsistencies limit the gain: Section 4.5 claims acceptance above 85% for brightness ×2, but Table 2 reports 51.79%; the new heterogeneous-message curves also fall below the blanket ≥0.96 robustness statement. Overall, the added evidence provides a useful but qualified improvement.
